name: spatialite-tools
why: Command-line access to spatial SQLite databases; a real door into GIS with an unusual twist on SQLite.

brief.what_it_is: spatialite-tools is a collection of open source command-line tools for SpatiaLite, the spatial extension for SQLite. The main tool, spatialite, is a full CLI front-end comparable to sqlite3 but with SpatiaLite support. Other tools import and export Shapefiles and DBF files, check shapefiles for anomalies, load EXIF/GPS metadata from JPEG pictures, import GML and DXF files, build routing networks, process OpenStreetMap data, and handle XML files. The homepage does not say explicitly what each tool emits beyond these import, export, and conversion descriptions.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage describes it simply as a collection of CLI tools supporting SpatiaLite. The XML tools were funded by the Tuscany Region's Territorial and Environmental Information System, which is the only stated motivation beyond the tools themselves.
brief.install_notes: The homepage offers source tarballs (spatialite-tools-5.1.0a.tar.gz and .zip). It does not describe build steps, dependencies, or first-run configuration. It lists strictly related projects: libspatialite, spatialite_gui, FreeXL, ReadOSM, and VirtualPG. Building it likely needs libspatialite, but the homepage does not say so.
brief.standout: It is a suite of about twenty small command-line tools covering shapefiles, OSM, XML, GML, DXF, EXIF, and routing, all built around SpatiaLite. It turns a SQLite database into a GIS workbench from the shell, and the spatialite front-end is a full SpatiaLite-aware replacement for sqlite3.
brief.status: Last release on the homepage is 5.1.0a, dated 2023-08-13. The homepage shows no newer release and gives no commit or activity data. The Fossil footer is dated 2020, which only reflects the Fossil software version. Beyond the release date I cannot tell whether it is maintained.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not state platform support or build requirements. The version is labelled 'a', which suggests an alpha or pre-release. The brew entry has no caveats. The homepage has no usage examples, so the tool behaviour is only described at a headline level.

judge.reason: SpatiaLite makes SQLite a spatial database, and this suite opens that up through GIS imports, OSM processing, routing, and a spatially aware SQL shell.

entry.title: spatialite-tools
entry.tldr: A bundle of about twenty command-line tools that turn SQLite into a GIS workbench: shapefiles, OpenStreetMap, GPS photos and routing networks, all in one database file.
entry.deeper_look:
spatialite-tools is the command-line companion to SpatiaLite, a spatial extension for SQLite. The main tool, `spatialite`, is described as "a complete CLI front-end, more or less equivalent to the well known sqlite3 front-end, but fully supporting SpatiaLite". You get the familiar SQLite shell, with geometry types and spatial functions available.

The other executables are small single-purpose converters and checkers. They import and export Shapefiles and DBF files, check shapefiles for anomalies, load EXIF/GPS metadata from JPEG pictures, import GML and DXF files, build routing networks, process OpenStreetMap data, and handle XML. The XML tools were funded by the Tuscany Region's Territorial and Environmental Information System.

The idea underneath is that a spatial database does not have to be a server. A whole map dataset can live in one SQLite file that you copy around, query with SQL, and feed from the shell. If GIS has seemed like heavy desktop software, this is a way in that looks like a pipeline of small Unix tools.

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options of the SpatiaLite-aware SQLite shell.
Shows the options of the general import and export tool for shapefiles, DBF and similar formats.
Shows how to load EXIF and GPS metadata from JPEG pictures into a database.

entry.whats_unique: It is a whole suite of small converters around one idea, SQL for maps in a single SQLite file, and its shell is a drop-in replacement for sqlite3.
entry.caveats: The homepage has no usage examples or build notes, and the last release listed is 5.1.0a from August 2023, so expect to learn it from --help and the SpatiaLite docs.
